sections.html:
Concord is New Hampshire's capital and the seat of Merrimack County. Population is 44,597, and the city covers 67.19 square miles, so a Concord address can mean a downtown apartment, a village farmhouse or a lot on a back road. Manchester lies about 16 miles south and Boston 66 miles south.

Downtown includes the North End and South End neighborhoods, and four villages sit around it:

  • Penacook
  • Concord Heights
  • East Concord
  • West Concord

Most homes fall in the Concord School District. Penacook is served by the Merrimack Valley School District and carries a higher tax rate, shown in the next section. Interstates 89 and 93 meet just south of the city, I-393 runs east toward the Seacoast, and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport is 23 miles south. Many buyers here work for the state or the hospital, so commute and move-in timing often drive their offers.

sections.h2: Tax rate, ratio and assessing office
sections.html:
Concord's tax year runs April 1 to March 31. The 2025 equalization ratio is 60.4%, which means assessed values sit well below what homes sell for. Dividing a total assessed value by that ratio gives a rough market value.

2025 property tax rates by area
AreaRate per $1,000 of assessed valueSchool district
Concord (most of the city)$29.11Concord School District
Penacook$30.74Merrimack Valley School District

The last citywide update before 2026 took effect April 1, 2021. Concord then carried out a full revaluation for tax year 2026, with Vision Government Solutions doing the field and data work. Your new value may differ a lot from the old one, and the rate moves too, so do not multiply a new assessment by last year's rate to guess your bill. Late payments carry interest at 8%, prorated daily.

The assessing office is at 41 Green Street, phone 603-225-8550. Call there with questions about your property record card, square footage or the condition notes on your house.

File an abatement application with the city by March 1 following the final tax bill. Abatements can be granted for good cause, usually an assessment error or a disproportionate assessment. The municipality has until July 1 to grant or deny the request. If you disagree with the answer, you can appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to superior court, but not both, no later than September 1.

Filing does not stop collection, so pay the bill as assessed. If an abatement is granted, a refund with interest follows. A complaint that taxes are too high will not succeed on its own. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal.

  1. Pull your property record card and check it for errors in size, age or features.
  2. Gather recent sales of similar Concord homes.
  3. Talk with the assessing office first.
  4. File the abatement application by March 1.
  5. Wait for the written answer, due by July 1.
  6. Appeal by September 1 if you still disagree.

sections.h2: What a Concord seller pays at closing
sections.html:
New Hampshire's real estate transfer tax is $.75 per $100 of the sale price, and the statute charges it to both the buyer and the seller under RSA 78-B. Filing and payment go through the state's Granite Tax Connect portal. Your purchase agreement and the title company set out how the split is handled.

Expect these items on the settlement statement:

  • Transfer tax under RSA 78-B
  • Unpaid property tax for the current tax year
  • Any mortgage or lien payoff
  • Agent commission, if you list with an agent

Property tax is the other large line. Because the city's tax year starts April 1, ask your closing agent how the current year will be prorated between you and the buyer. Deeds are recorded at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds, 163 N Main Street, Concord, phone (603) 228-0101. Bring a copy of your deed, your latest tax bill and your mortgage payoff request to the first meeting with the closing office.

For a one to four family home, New Hampshire law requires a written seller disclosure before or during the preparation of an offer. RSA 477:4-d covers the private water supply, the private sewage system, insulation, flood hazard zone status and any underground heating oil tank.

If you do not know the answer on water, sewage or insulation, you have to say so in writing. The buyer signs to acknowledge receipt. A separate rule, RSA 477:4-c, applies before any purchase contract that includes a building. It asks for details such as the system's age, its last service date and the contractor who services it. Use the current version of the form, and complete it before you accept an offer so nothing delays the contract.

Many Concord houses are old, and some still have original wiring, plaster walls or a stone foundation. Winters are long, cold and snowy, so a buyer's inspector will look hard at a few things:

  • The roof and its ability to carry a heavy snow load
  • The heating system, its age and its fuel type
  • Pipes, insulation and any sign of water intrusion
  • The foundation and drainage after spring melt

Deferred work in these areas is a common reason a financed sale stalls. A cash buyer who purchases as-is does not ask you to fix them first.

A Concord house can sell while taxes are unpaid. The balance, with interest, comes out of your proceeds at closing. Ask the city for a current figure before you sign a contract, and give the title company your most recent bill so the next installment is credited to the right owner.

Check the timing as well. A closing just before or just after a billing date changes who owes what for the period, and a quick conversation with your closing agent settles it. If you also owe a mortgage or a lien, the payoff letters should be ordered early.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works for a Concord house
sections.html:
A cash sale replaces the lender's appraisal and underwriting with a direct purchase, so the timeline depends on title work and your own schedule. You describe the house, receive an offer, and decide whether to accept. Nothing is owed if you decline.

The transfer tax, the property tax proration and the disclosure form still apply to a cash deal. What changes is that you skip repairs, showings and the financing contingency. That helps if you own an older house with a tired roof or heating system, or if you are settling an estate and need a firm closing date.

Before you accept any offer, confirm the closing date, who pays which closing costs and whether the buyer takes the house with everything left inside it.

faqs.q: Is Concord's property tax rate the same everywhere in the city?
faqs.a: No. The 2025 rate is $29.11 per $1,000 for most of Concord and $30.74 for Penacook, which is served by the Merrimack Valley School District.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal a Concord assessment?
faqs.a: The abatement application is due by March 1 following the final tax bill. The city has until July 1 to respond, and any further appeal must be filed by September 1.

faqs.q: Do both the buyer and the seller pay New Hampshire's transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes, the statute imposes $.75 per $100 of the price on each of them. Your purchase agreement and title company set out who pays what at closing.

faqs.q: Does Concord have a revaluation affecting my sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Concord completed a full revaluation for tax year 2026, and the last citywide update before it took effect April 1, 2021. New values can change a buyer's tax estimate, so check your own notice.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Concord house with a private well or septic system?
faqs.a: Yes, but you must give the buyer the written water and sewage disclosure under RSA 477:4-d. If you do not know an answer, the law requires you to say so in writing.
